name: Indigo hair dye

card.summary: A plant dye from Indigofera leaves, usually used after henna, to turn hair from red or orange to dark brown or black.
card.aka: Indigo powder, basma, natural black dye
card.note: Pure indigo is distinct from PPD-adulterated "black henna", which can cause severe allergic reactions.

quick.overview:
Indigo hair dye is powdered indigo plant leaf, mainly from Indigofera tinctoria. Mixed with henna it yields brown and black shades, and it is used by people who want dark hair without synthetic dye.

Henna alone gives red-orange; adding indigo shifts the colour toward brown or black. The dye has a long history, being called nila in Sanskrit and basma in Iran.
quick.how: People mix the powder with water and apply it to hair, commonly after or combined with henna. Shade depends on the ratio and the hair. Natural indigo is applied in a leuco (colourless) form that oxidises to blue.
quick.risks: Pure indigo is a plant product, but hair colouring in general can cause allergic reactions. Products sold as "black henna" may contain PPD, which can cause severe reactions and lifelong sensitivity.

lead: Indigo hair dye is powdered leaf of Indigofera tinctoria and related plants, used to turn hair dark brown or black with a plant-based colourant. Fermenting the leaves converts the glycoside indican into indigotin, the blue pigment. [1]

On its own indigo gives blue-toned results, so it is normally paired with henna. Henna stains hair orange to auburn, and Wikipedia notes it can be mixed with indigo for brown and black shades. [2] People who want dark hair without synthetic oxidative dyes use the henna-then-indigo or henna-indigo combination for this reason. [2][3]

The practice is old: Wikipedia's hair-colouring article lists henna and indigo among plant dyes recorded in ancient sources such as the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE). [3] Research specific to indigo on hair is sparse; most published material covers indigo as a textile dye, henna as a body and hair dye, and the safety of hair dyes in general. [3][4]

chain: Indigo layered or mixed in adds blue pigment
angle.text: Indigo is used to darken hair to brown or black with a plant dye, normally alongside henna.

paras: Natural indigo is made by soaking and fermenting leaves, then mixing the precipitate with a strong base such as lye. Most indigo produced today is synthetic, but plant dye is still sold as a natural colorant under names such as tarum (Indonesia), nila (Malaysia and Sanskrit) and basma (Iran and parts of the former Soviet Union). [1]

Chemically, the plant precursor indican is a colourless, water-soluble tryptophan derivative. During soaking it releases indoxyl, which forms yellow leucoindigo; exposure to air oxidises this to insoluble blue indigo. That is why indigo-dyed material turns blue as it dries, and why Wikipedia describes indigo as generally applied to hair in its colourless leuco form. [3][4]

Henna on its own produces orange, auburn or burgundy tones depending on the starting colour and the quality of the henna. [2] Adding indigo, either mixed in or applied as a second step, moves the result toward brown and black. [2] Wikipedia also records that henna can be blended with Cassia obovata for lighter reds or blonds, so indigo is one of several plant additions used to steer shade. [2]
Some products sold as henna contain other natural dyes, metal salts, oils or waxes that change how the dye takes, or dyes that can cause allergies, so labels vary in what they actually contain. [2]

India was the earliest major centre of indigo cultivation and the chief supplier to Europe from Greco-Roman times; the English word derives from the Greek indikon and Latin indicum. [4] The oldest known indigo-dyed fabric, about 6,000 years old, was found at Huaca Prieta in Peru. [4]

Marco Polo in the 13th century was the first European to report on indigo preparation in India. [1] Adolf von Baeyer worked out indigo synthesis between 1865 and 1883, and BASF had a commercially viable process by 1897; plant-based output fell from about 19,000 tons in 1897 to about 1,000 tons by 1914. [4]
The name black henna dates to the late 19th century, when partly fermented indigo was sold under that name for dyeing hair black. [2]

Today the term black henna more often describes pastes that contain para-phenylenediamine (PPD), a chemical used in hair dyes. Henna artists began using PPD pastes for body art in the 1990s because they stain skin quickly. [2] Wikipedia says such pastes can cause severe allergic reactions, blistering and permanent scarring, with reactions sometimes appearing 3 to 12 days after application and sensitisation that can last for life. [2][5]

The same article notes that indigo does not dye skin black, and that hair dye products must keep PPD below 6% while black henna pastes have been found with 10% to 80%. [2] The US FDA has not approved henna for direct application to skin, and treats henna as grandfathered for use as a hair dye. [2]

Hair colouring in general can cause redness, itching and burning, sometimes appearing a day later; manufacturers often recommend a patch test, while some European dermatologists have advised against pre-use testing. [3] Dyes can stain skin and nails near the hairline, usually fading within a week. [3]

Indigo itself has low oral toxicity, with an LD50 of about 5 g/kg in mammals. [4] Henna is reported as dangerous for people with G6PD deficiency, particularly infants and children from the Middle East and North Africa. [2]
No studies found. Published human research on indigo concerns other uses, for example indigo naturalis in ulcerative colitis, and not hair colouring.

timeline.event: The Egyptian Ebers Papyrus describes dyeing grey hair; henna and indigo are among the plants used in ancient hair colouring. [3]
Marco Polo reports on indigo preparation in India. [1]
Adolf von Baeyer works on indigo synthesis and fixes its structure in 1883. [4]
Partly fermented indigo is sold as black henna for dyeing hair. [2]
BASF has an economically viable synthetic indigo process. [4]
PPD-based pastes begin to be sold as black henna body art. [2]
